eras.title: Basement and Country
eras.summary: After his 1966 motorcycle accident Dylan stopped touring, settled with his family near Woodstock and recorded informally with the Band in a basement. He re-emerged with quiet, country-tinged records made in Nashville, trading the electric storm of the mid-sixties for plain songs about love, home and old America.

moments.title: Motorcycle accident near Woodstock
moments.text: In late July 1966 Dylan crashed his Triumph motorcycle near his home in Woodstock, New York, and afterwards stopped touring for years.

moments.title: Woodstock: basement sessions with the Hawks
moments.text: Through 1967 Dylan recorded dozens of informal songs with members of the Hawks, soon to be the Band, in the basement of a house called Big Pink near Woodstock.

moments.title: Isle of Wight Festival
moments.text: On August 31, 1969, backed by the Band, he headlined the Isle of Wight Festival in England, his first full-length concert since 1966.

moments.title: Honorary doctorate from Princeton
moments.text: In June 1970 Princeton University gave him an honorary Doctor of Music degree, a day he later turned into a song on New Morning.

albums.title: John Wesley Harding
albums.why: Released in late 1967 after more than a year of silence, it swapped the wild electric sound of 1966 for spare Nashville recordings with a tiny band. Its short, biblical parables about outlaws, drifters and saints set the quiet tone for the rest of his country years.

albums.title: Nashville Skyline
albums.why: Recorded in Nashville and released in 1969, it showed Dylan singing in a smooth croon few listeners recognized. Its brief country love songs, a duet with Johnny Cash and the hit Lay Lady Lay helped bring rock and country audiences together.

albums.title: Self Portrait
albums.why: A 1970 double album made mostly of covers, traditional songs and a few live tracks, it baffled critics and fans expecting new Dylan songs. Later reissues of its sessions earned it a kinder reassessment.

albums.title: New Morning
albums.why: Arriving only months after Self Portrait, it was welcomed as a return to original songwriting with warm, domestic songs about family and country life.

songs.title: John Wesley Harding
songs.note: The title track is loosely based on the Texas outlaw John Wesley Hardin, with an extra letter added to the name.
songs.preview: A brisk ballad painting an outlaw as a friend of the poor who was never pinned down by the law.

songs.title: As I Went Out One Morning
songs.note: Like most of the album, it was cut in Nashville in late 1967 with just bass, drums and Dylan's guitar and harmonica.
songs.preview: A walker meets a captive young woman who begs to go south with him, until a figure of authority intervenes.

songs.title: I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine
songs.note: Its title and opening echo the labor ballad about the union organizer Joe Hill.
songs.preview: A dream of a grieving saint ends with the dreamer waking in shame over his own part in the saint's fate.

songs.title: All Along the Watchtower
songs.note: It became Dylan's most performed song in concert, usually played in the hard-rock arrangement Hendrix gave it.
songs.preview: Two outsiders talk on the road while, from a high lookout, the powerful watch riders approaching through the wind.

songs.title: Drifter’s Escape
songs.note: A three-minute parable that closes the first side of the original LP.
songs.preview: A bewildered man on trial slips away when a bolt from the sky strikes the courthouse.

songs.title: The Wicked Messenger
songs.note: At about two minutes it is one of the shortest songs on the album.
songs.preview: A messenger who twists every report is told to bring only good news if he must speak at all.

songs.title: I’ll Be Your Baby Tonight
songs.note: Pete Drake's pedal steel on the closing track pointed toward the country sound of Nashville Skyline.
songs.preview: A relaxed invitation to drop all worries and spend the night together.

songs.title: Girl From the North Country
songs.note: Dylan re-recorded his 1963 song as a duet with Johnny Cash in Nashville, and it opens the album.
songs.preview: Two old voices recall a lost love up north and ask a traveler to check that she is warm and well.

songs.title: Nashville Skyline Rag
songs.note: An instrumental that lets the Nashville session players take the spotlight.
songs.preview: A wordless, upbeat country romp built around picking solos.

songs.title: To Be Alone With You
songs.note: A spoken aside from Dylan to producer Bob Johnston was left in at the start of the track.
songs.preview: A cheerful song of counting down the day until the singer can be alone with his sweetheart.

songs.title: I Threw It All Away
songs.note: Dylan sang it on the premiere episode of The Johnny Cash Show in 1969.
songs.preview: A man admits he carelessly gave up the love he had and warns others not to do the same.

songs.title: Lay Lady Lay
songs.note: Released as a single, it reached the US top ten in 1969.
songs.preview: A soft, crooned plea for a lover to stay the night.

songs.title: Tell Me That It Isn't True
songs.note: It was recorded in Nashville in February 1969 with Bob Johnston producing.
songs.preview: A man hears rumors that his lover has left him for someone else and begs her to deny them.

songs.title: Tonight I'll Be Staying Here With You
songs.note: It closes the album and was also issued as a single.
songs.preview: A traveler throws away his ticket and decides to stay with the woman he loves instead of moving on.

songs.title: All the Tired Horses
songs.note: The album's opening track is sung entirely by female backing singers, with no lead vocal from Dylan.
songs.preview: A short, repeated chant about a rider unable to get going while the day passes.

songs.title: Copper Kettle
songs.note: A 1950s song by Albert Frank Beddoe about making moonshine, earlier recorded by Joan Baez.
songs.preview: An old-timer praises brewing whiskey in the hills, far from tax collectors.

songs.title: The Boxer
songs.note: Dylan covered Paul Simon's song by harmonizing with his own overdubbed voice in two different singing styles.
songs.preview: A poor young man who came to the city looking for work tells of hard times while a fighter keeps going despite every blow.

songs.title: If Not for You
songs.note: George Harrison recorded it the same year for All Things Must Pass.
songs.preview: A grateful love song saying the world would be gray and empty without the beloved.

songs.title: Day of the Locusts
songs.note: It recalls the day he accepted an honorary degree at Princeton in June 1970, when cicadas filled the air.
songs.preview: An uneasy man sits through a stuffy ceremony and is glad to escape back to the hills with his love.

songs.title: The Man in Me
songs.note: It plays over the opening credits of the 1998 film The Big Lebowski.
songs.preview: A man says only the right woman can see past his defenses to who he really is.

songs.title: All Along the Watchtower
songs.note: The Jimi Hendrix Experience's version on Electric Ladyland became a hit single in 1968.

songs.title: If Not for You
songs.note: George Harrison's version appeared on his 1970 triple album All Things Must Pass.

links.why: Hendrix recorded his electric version within months of the original's release, and Dylan later adopted its arrangement on stage.
George Harrison released his own version on All Things Must Pass in the same year Dylan put the song out.
